title: Second observer on f69v: 28 bars strictly alternating dark and pale, which the 28 radial labels do not echo; the drawing alone cannot separate one mansion list from another, and the Bodleian comparison was not reachable from this seat
statement: A second visual pass for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, region 1300,1080,1250,1250 at full resolution). Exposure: I had read the step statement, so I knew the earlier count of 28 and the claimed 14/14 alternation before looking; this is an independent recount, not a blind one. I read no glyph values and no words of the transcription; from it I took only line ids and unit codes. What I see: 28 bars radiate from a central disc, each ending in a green oval cap. Going clockwise from the bar nearest 12 o'clock I coded each bar as dark blue or pale grey-green: D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P, that is 14 dark and 14 pale with no break in the alternation anywhere round the circle. The dark bars are also the longer ones (their caps sit further out) and the pale bars the shorter, without exception, so length and colour are one feature, not two. The eleventh bar clockwise (about 4 o'clock) is a darker, greener blue than the other dark bars; I cannot tell paint variation from intent. The central disc is cut by pale yellow curved arms into wedges, about six or seven (I could not fix the number), filled with blue wash and small stars in unequal numbers, one wedge at the top solid blue-green with almost no stars. Outside the bars stand short radial words, one beyond each bar as far as I can see; the transcription has exactly 28 lines of the radial unit (f69v.4 to f69v.31), matching the bar count, and three circular text lines (f69v.1 to 3). Faint blue lines continue outward from some bars into the text rings, roughly eight of them, unevenly spaced. Consequence for the test the step asks for: apart from the count, the only ordered visual feature of the 28 loci is a two-state alternation. Under any rotation and either direction a tradition's list can be laid on it in only two distinguishable ways (which parity is dark), so the picture can at most test a prediction of the form 'odd-numbered mansions differ from even-numbered ones in some named property'; it cannot rank Middle Persian, Arabic and Latin lists against each other. Any tradition-specific evidence has to come from the 28 radial labels, compared in order, and the eleventh bar is the only candidate for a visual origin mark, a weak one. Not done: the masked comparison with Bodleian MS Bodl. Or. 133. The Bodleian image server is blocked for this seat, so I did not see those scans and code nothing about them. Before learning that, and before looking at any image, I fixed this feature list for whoever can reach both: number of equal radial divisions; whether divisions alternate in two tones; whether each division carries its own written name; number of concentric bands of writing; centre motif; dot or star groups of varying count and whether they sit in the divisions or in the centre; divisions as rays from the centre or as cells of a ring; visible grouping of divisions into larger named sets; figurative drawings in the divisions. My f69v codes: 28; yes; yes (28 radial words); 3; disc with curved arms and star-filled wedges; yes, in the centre only; rays; none visible; none. Addition, a text check that follows from the above: if the two-state alternation of the bars meant something about the 28 items, the 28 radial labels might alternate too. I fixed three statistics before running anything and ran them once: the difference in mean label length (glyphs) between labels at odd and even positions; and, for the first glyph and for the last glyph, the number of positions whose glyph equals the one two places on minus the number equal to the one next to it, round the circle. Null: the same 28 labels in shuffled order, 20,000 shuffles. Position parity does not depend on where the transcription starts or which way it runs, so no alignment had to be chosen. ZL3b loci f69v.4 to 31: length difference 0.07 glyphs (p = 1.00), first-glyph excess -1 (p = 0.71), last-glyph excess -5 (p = 0.99). IT2a gives the same and RF1b the same except a last-glyph excess of -4 (p = 0.97); GC2a gives 0.36 (p = 0.39), -1 (p = 0.71), -3 (p = 0.93). Power: adding one glyph to every label on one parity of a shuffled ring is detected at p < 0.05 in 157 of 200 trials, so the length test would have seen a one-glyph alternation about four times in five; the first-glyph test is weak because 20 of the 28 labels begin with the same glyph. So the labels show no period-two pattern to go with the bars: on this evidence the dark and pale bars do not mark two classes of label.
check: Another seat codes the same nine features on the two Bodleian scans named in P-L4-002 and on at least two control diagrams that are not mansion diagrams (for example a 12-fold calendar wheel and another Voynich wheel), with captions hidden, and counts feature agreements with my f69v codes; f69v supports the mansion reading only if the Bodleian diagram agrees on more features than every control once the count of 28 is set aside. Separately, anyone may recount the bars on the region cited and compare the clockwise D/P sequence and the odd eleventh bar.
